title: Reginald's Gnome Rescue Mission
markdown:
Reginald Rat, Esq., paused, quill hovering over a neatly lined notebook. Beside him the grand tiled expanse of the municipal swimming baths shimmered. The air echoed with splashes and the happy shouts of children on summer holiday. Reginald was a gardener at heart, and even on his day off his mind buzzed with plans. Today’s list, a masterpiece of neat columns titled Grand Summer Bathhouse Bloom Survey, included Species Observed, Water Proximity, and Sunlight Exposure. He was especially proud of his system for spotting the most water-loving ferns.

A twitch in his whiskers said not everything was going to schedule. He had been admiring a patch of bright green moss near the busy changing rooms, imagining it a tiny damp forest, when his elbow—perhaps a bit too enthusiastic—nudged a small chipped ceramic gnome. It did not fall with a crash. It made a soft wet plop into the shallow end of the main pool. A small mistake, he told himself. A tiny oops. The trouble was the Head Lifeguard, Brenda, a woman with a whistle sharp enough to curdle milk from fifty paces, was rather fond of that particular gnome. And lunch, Reginald’s most important midday ritual, was in forty-five minutes. The list stated, in bold underlined letters: Item 7: Fix any problems before lunch.

His secret flaw, the one he never wrote down, was making simple fixes into big complicated messes when he got flustered. His tail twitched. “Oh dear, oh dear. Brenda will have my whiskers. She guards that gnome like solid gold.” He needed a real plan. He had already written Plan A: Get the gnome. Staring at it bobbing innocently, the line felt completely useless.

Nell the tortoise ambled up. Her ancient shell-patterned head emerged slowly, like the sun. “Good morning, Reginald. Admiring the moss? Or thinking about garden ornaments taking a dip?”

“Nell. Just… surveying.” He tried to smooth his whiskers. His heart thumped a drum solo. “A small, yet important, thing has happened. A garden ornament has, shall we say, entered the water. It needs to be moved. Quietly. Before lunch.”

Nell blinked wise slow eyes that seemed to hold a thousand quiet afternoons. “Move it. Yes. A sensible idea. Are we going for a swim first, or is getting the gnome out the main event?”

“Swim?” He squeaked. “No, no, no. We must get it first. The lunch bell is ticking. Forty-five minutes is ages for a worried rat.” He scribbled. “Plan B: Operation Gnome Rescue. Requires extreme quiet and maybe a long net.”

A group of children, faces red from playing, giggled past. “Look, it’s Reginald the Rat and his super-slow friend.”

He winced, fur prickling. He just needed to get the gnome out, dry it with the emergency handkerchief, and put it back on its mossy spot as if it had never left. A discarded pool noodle lay near the lifeguard’s chair—perfect for nudging closer, then a quick scoop with his hat. He began to tiptoe, trying to look as if he were merely strolling.

“He means,” Nell stated calmly to the giggling children, her voice carrying, “that Reginald is going to lead a very special and unique water game. Like a competitive gnome-fishing contest. He is very good at organizing things.”

Their eyes widened. Giggles became excited whispers. “Gnome-fishing. Can we play? Is it a race?”

Reginald froze mid-tiptoe. Gnome-fishing? That was not the plan. Not even a little. Plan B was already turning public and chaotic. The children dashed off to find their parents, shouting about the competition.

“Nell, you didn’t.”

“It is rather floaty,” Nell observed, nodding at the gnome. “And you are very clever. I am sure you will find a way.”

His mind raced: what-ifs and oh-noses. Children gathered in groups, voices a rising tide of strategies. Some planned towel nets. Others suggested luring the gnome with biscuit crumbs. Complete disaster. Brenda would hear, see the rogue gnome, and then—he shuddered—the long list of punishments. He had to hide it before the lunchtime rush.

His panicked eyes found the overflow drain at the far end, partly underwater. A determined push and the gnome would disappear into the pipes before anyone could say gnome. He dashed, heart pounding, intending a quiet vanishing.

A small boy ran toward him, face beaming, holding a bright blue pool noodle like a trophy. “Mr Rat. My mum said I could give you this. For the gnome-fishing. She said it would help.”

Despair. Lists, clever plans, hopes for a calm afternoon—dissolving like sugar in hot tea. He stood by the pool with a noodle, a gnome bobbing toward the drain, and a crowd of excited children. Nell offered a slow encouraging smile that seemed to say: you can do this, old friend.

This was the moment. He could not get it out quietly. He could not hide it. He looked at the noodle, then the gnome, and with a sigh that rustled his whiskers and sent dust motes dancing, he made a decision that was not written down and felt, somehow, right. He nudged the gnome not toward the drain but toward the shallow steps. He placed the noodle beside it like a gentle helper.

He walked back to the notebook and, with a flourish that surprised even himself, tore out the Grand Summer Bathhouse Bloom Survey and the increasingly frantic Plans A, B, and C. He crumpled the page and tossed it into a bin with a satisfying thud.

“Nell. It seems my plan has changed. It is not about hiding a mistake anymore. It is about playing together. Fixing things as a team.”

He dipped a paw into the cool water, a welcome relief against suddenly warm fur, and nudged the gnome further onto the steps. The children, seeing him take action, let out a collective cheer. He guided them—not a frantic contest, but a careful cooperative lift.

“Gently now, everyone. Let’s help our little friend. He looks quite wet. Perhaps he needs a nice warm place to dry.”

Nell watched, contented. The careful list-maker had found a far more joyful project than any perfectly finished column. Happy laughter, shared effort, the simple act of fixing an accident together: better than any completed list.

Brenda the Head Lifeguard strode over, formidable whistle ready, eyes sweeping the scene. Reginald braced, fur bristling. Instead of a scolding she looked at the retrieved gnome, the smiling children, and the slightly damp rat.

“Well now.” A hint of a smile, a rare sight. “Looks like you lot have saved the day. Quite an organised effort.” She winked, a gesture of shared understanding. “Perhaps you could add Emergency Gnome Rescue to your gardening duties next year. Seems you have a knack.”

His fur still smelled of pool water and sunshine. The feeling in his chest was not the neat click of a ticked item. It was warmer. He looked at Nell, who gave a knowing nod, then at the children reverently placing the gnome back on its mossy perch. He still loved his lists. From that day, he suspected, some of the most important entries would be found not on paper, but in the doing.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
